newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Grain trade mostly off hook after EU award.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Grain trade mostly off hook after EU award.

text.p: Grain traders breathed a collective sigh of relief on Thursday as the European Union sold more wheat than expected at auction -- but a few will be nursing wounds after bidding for too low a level of subsidy, exporters said.

Traders had been bracing for an agonising New Year break without the volume of licences they needed to cover existing deals after the EU's agriculture director, Guy Legras, threatened to clamp down on exports earlier this week.
But the 400,000 tonnes of soft wheat released for export from the EU market, close to the previous week's record for the season, will keep most traders happy over Christmas.
"It should have covered the shorts in the market," one major exporter said of the award.
"If anyone isn't covered now, it's their own fault."
The EU's cereals management committee awarded licences for 397,500 tonnes of open market common, or soft, wheat at a maximum rebate of 11.94 Ecu per tonne, officials said.
It also granted 237,500 tonnes of open market barley at a maximum refund of 28.99 Ecus in its weekly export tender.
Traders said they were relieved by the volume of wheat exports, which was nearly double the 200,000 tonnes most operators had been expecting.
Up to 500,000 tonnes of wheat is said to have been sold short without the cover of EU export certificates.
Legras sent shockwaves through the market last Friday when he said the EU was thinking about "turning the screw" on exports after selling a million tonnes in the previous two weeks.

The remarks, which Legras reaffirmed on Monday, encouraged some traders to bid aggressively for licences at subsidy levels well below 10 Ecus per tonne in a move many interpreted as an effort to snap up the few licences likely to be awarded.
Industry sources said a handful of firms accounted for the first 200,000 tonnes of wheat sought at 7.49 to 9.42 Ecus.
"It's more than Legras had promised," said one exporter, pleased that higher bids above 10 Ecus per tonne had also been included in the EU licence award.
A grain official from an EU member country said the European Commission had wanted to cover existing sales and head off what some officials regarded as a squeeze play on export licences.
"The people who were bidding seven Ecus tried to block all the restitutions and they lost," he said.
A strong volume of bids at a low refund level would encourage the Commission to set the cut-off for subsidies in single figures and leave some exporters short of licences.
Some traders however felt the award, pricing wheat at $160 per tonne for the highest subsidy, still left EU wheat uncompetitive and called for a higher refund still.
"It's still not competitive with Argentine wheat at $151," one exporter said.
Despite concerns about weather disruption in Argentina, the country still has a heavy crop and Australia is looking at an excellent harvest, he said.
Traders said none of the licences would be held for the long term, even though licences given now are valid until end-April.
"These quantities are to cover sales in January," said one.
The barley award reflected aggressive bidding, according to one export specialist for the grain. He put French barley at around $136 per tonne based on the tender results.
The barley exports were likely to be headed for Saudi Arabia amid widespread speculation of a new raid by the world's largest barley importer on the grain market within days.
Shippers said the assumption was Riyadh would be back in the market before the next EU tender on January 9.
-- Chris Lyddon, Tim Hepher, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
